title: Universality and Convergence of Generative Flows

paper.title: Universality and Convergence of Generative Flows
paper.abstract:
Abstract Generative flows sample from an unnormalized target by training a flow to be balanced, and the
training loss is the signal a practitioner watches. We ask what that signal is worth: whether a
small loss certifies an accurate sampler, whether the loss can be driven to zero, and how fast
gradient descent does so. The loss decides the first. Losses that compare the two sides of the
balance by their difference bound, in total variation, the error of the sampler the flow implies,
with explicit constants that do not involve the policy; flow-matching losses that compare them
through a ratio admit no such bound, already on a single cycle, whenever their generator is
continuous at balance. On graphs, the backward policy decides the other two. Once it is frozen,
balance becomes invariance under the backward chain, so that existence is free on finite graphs, and
one constant — the norm of that chain’s Green operator, which plays the role of an inverse spectral
gap — fixes the order of the curvature of the loss around the balanced flow, from above and below,
and sets a floor under the rate at which training converges near it. The mechanism is that gradient descent diffuses the flow along the
backward policy. For the squared-logarithm generator of detailed and trajectory balance, training the
balance loss on states converges globally on every finite path-connected graph, from every positive
initialization. The constant can be infinite while backward trajectories are short on average, and
exact flow matching can then fail. The bounds and rates are tested by exact computation on
enumerable state spaces, and every theorem carries a certification status computed from a Lean 4
development.

sections.heading: 1.1 Generative flows and the cost of mixing
sections.text: A generative flow or GFlowNet ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Bengio et al., 2023 ) was originally defined on a directed acyclic graph as a positive weighting of its edges, called a flow. It defines a sampling process for an unnormalized target distribution on the vertices: it starts from some initial distribution on the vertices and, at each vertex, chooses between following an edge and stopping (which we see as following an edge toward a sink state, weighted by the reward), with probabilities proportional to the flow. The fundamental result of GFlowNets states that when the flow is balanced — at every state, what arrives or starts equals what leaves or stops — the stopped state is an exact sample of the target ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Bengio et al., 2023 ) . Training enforces balance through a loss: flow matching, detailed balance, trajectory balance and their variants ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Bengio et al., 2023 ; Whitammer et al., 2022 ; Pan et al., 2023 ; Madan et al., 2023 ; da Silva et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2025 ) . Built on directed acyclic graphs, the framework now covers continuous state spaces ( Li et al., 2023 ; Lahlou et al., 2023 ) , state spaces with cycles ( Brunswic et al., 2024 ; Brunswic et al., 2025a ; Morozov et al., 2025 ) and multiple agents ( Brunswic et al., 2025b ) , and the models it fine-tunes are moving the same way. Generative flows fine-tune autoregressive models, whose generation explores a tree ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Takase et al., 2024 ; Ho et al., 2024 ; Bartoldson et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) ; diffusion language models unmask tokens in any order and some revise them ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Nie et al., 2025 ; von Rütte et al., 2025 ) , so a state is reached along many paths and, where tokens are revised, along cycles. In their seminal work, Bengio et al. (2021) explain that GFlowNets are expected to escape the cost of mixing that burdens Markov chain Monte Carlo ( Levin & Peres, 2017 ) during inference . A common informal belief is that the choice of the frozen backward policy used in the detailed-balance and trajectory-balance losses matters for the convergence of training ( Gritsaev et al., 2025 ) . Whoever trains a generative flow watches a loss and needs three things from it: that a small value certifies an accurate sampler, that the value can be driven to zero, and that gradient descent drives it there in reasonable time. Answers so far are partial: da Silva et al. (2025b) ; da Silva et al. (2025a) give guarantees on finite acyclic graphs, Brunswic et al. (2025a) bound the total-variation sampling error of any flow by its flow-matching defect and prove L 1 L^{1} -universality of ergodic flows, and Morozov et al. (2025) show that on a finite graph a positive frozen backward policy determines a unique balanced flow, so that the stability of the loss plays no role in where training goes. These last two works point the same way: holding a policy fixed is what makes universality and existence provable. The present work combines these ideas with the Markov-chain viewpoint of Deleu & Bengio (2023) into an encompassing framework that formalizes the intuition that frozen backward policies matter for training convergence; we provide convergence bounds controlling the sampling error by losses and describe the training dynamics in terms of a frozen backward policy. What a small loss certifies does not depend on the policy, and on finite graphs neither does existence; every rate of training does, through the mixing of the frozen backward chain and the ratio of the training measure to its invariant measure, and near balance that mixing constant bounds the curvature of the loss from both sides: GFlowNets do not escape the cost of mixing during training .

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: 1. Certificates and their limit (Section 2 ). We bound the sampling error by the stable and KL-weak-FM losses, with constants that do not involve the policy. We show that ratio-based flow matching with a generator continuous at 1 1 admits no such bound, already on one cycle. 2. The frozen chain (Section 3 ). We freeze the backward policy and wrap the graph around, so that balance is the invariance of one Markov chain. The norm B ^ \widehat{B} of that chain’s Green operator is the constant of the paper; it is a classical object ( Kemeny & Snell, 1960 ; Meyer, 1975 ; Meyer, 1980 ) , and what is new is its role in the curvature and the rate of training. 3. Existence (Section 4 ). On a finite path-connected graph a positive frozen backward policy admits, for each target positive on the stopping states, a balanced flow sampling it exactly, with no mixing hypothesis ( Morozov et al., 2025 ) ; we reprove it through the invariant measure of the loop closure ( Deleu & Bengio, 2023 ) and certify it. On a general state space, a frozen backward policy that mixes summably makes its flows universal in L p L^{p} . 4. Dynamics (Section 5 and Appendix B ). We show that gradient descent diffuses the flow along the frozen backward policy, that the curvature of the loss around the balanced flow is of order 1 / B ^ 2 1/\widehat{B}^{2} from both sides, and derive the local rate; for the generator ( log ⁡ x ) 2 (\log x)^{2} , training the balance loss on states converges from every positive initialization on every finite path-connected graph. We show that freezing does not give stability. 5. The boundary (Section 6 ). We give a counterexample, the doubling graph, on which the choice of the frozen backward policy alone decides whether a balanced flow exists and whether the constants of the bounds are finite. 6. A certified paper (Section 1.3 ). Every theorem of the paper is certified in Lean 4. Every theorem statement and badge is generated from the Lean certificate, and the whole development is unrolled in an appendix that opens on its proof-structure graph. With a fixed backward policy on a directed acyclic graph, learning a generative flow is entropy-regularized reinforcement learning ( Tiapkin et al., 2024 ; Deleu et al., 2024 ; Mohammadpour et al., 2024 ) , and entropy-regularized policy gradient converges globally at linear rates in tabular discounted Markov decision processes ( Mei et al., 2020 ; Cen et al., 2022 ) , and Morozov et al. (2025) extend the equivalence to graphs with cycles; the analysis here works in the space of flows, allows cycles and names the constant that sets the rate. Gritsaev et al. (2025) train the backward policy this paper freezes.

sections.heading: 1.2 Generative flows: framework and notation
sections.text: We work in the measurable theory of generative flows of Brunswic et al. (2024) , which admits cycles, in the reward-free form of Brunswic et al. (2025a) and Brunswic et al. (2025b) . One set of definitions then covers graphs, where the background measure is the counting measure, and continuous state spaces, where it is the Lebesgue or Riemannian volume; it is also the setting of the Lean development, whose sampler results hold on an arbitrary measurable space.

sections.heading: Stability.
sections.text: Brunswic et al. (2024) call a loss stable when adding a 0 0 -flow never lowers it, and the word is used here in that sense only. A 0 0 -flow adds the same measure to both sides of the balance. A difference does not see it; a ratio is pulled towards one. The difference losses ( 1 ) and ( 2 ) are therefore unchanged by a 0 0 -flow, while Brunswic et al. (2024) show that the ratio losses ( 3 )–( 5 ) are unstable: a circulation can lower them without changing what the sampler draws.

An arrow is solid when the Lean proof of its target runs through a module proving its source, dashed when the link is in the argument only; the full proof structure is drawn in the appendix. Figure 1 draws the argument; an arrow follows the order in which the story reaches a result. The sampling theorem answers the first question of Section 1.1 : forcing balance measures any flow against it and reduces certification to one norm of the balance defect, which difference losses control and ratio losses cannot. Freezing the backward policy answers the other two, once the graph is made a chain. The framework of Section 1.2 admits cycles, and the results on the frozen chain are proved for a Markov chain with an invariant measure, the ergodic presentation of generative flows ( Brunswic et al., 2025a ) that this paper adopts, and stated here on the graph. The acyclic graphs of practice reduce to it by a variant of the loop trick of Deleu & Bengio (2023) : wrap the graph around by an edge from the sink back to the source. On a finite path-connected graph the sampler’s trajectories, read backward, become the excursions of one irreducible chain, the balanced flow becomes its invariant measure, and cutting the wrap returns the acyclic flow, so the reduction loses nothing; what it adds, a chain that is never reversible and may be periodic, is why the constant is the norm B ^ \widehat{B} of the chain’s Green operator and not a spectral gap (Section 3 ). Balance is then the invariance of that chain, existence is free on finite graphs, and B ^ \widehat{B} is the cost of mixing that training pays: gradient descent, a diffusion along the backward policy, sees a curvature it bounds from both sides, a local rate it guarantees and, through hitting times, a guaranteed global one. The doubling graph closes the story where B ^ \widehat{B} is infinite.

sections.heading: Cited inputs (Section 1.2 ).
sections.text: Sampling theorem : a balanced flow samples its terminal flow exactly. Forcing balance : a flow that is not balanced, stopped by its implied terminal flow, samples with an error set by its initial defect; both certificates start there.

sections.heading: What a small loss certifies (Section 2 ).
sections.text: Stable losses certify the forced sampler, with a constant free of the policy. KL-weak-FM certifies it from samples of the target, to leading order by the square root of the loss’s excess over the target’s self-entropy. Ratio losses cannot : flow matching with a generator continuous at 1 1 is blind to circulations, and already on one cycle, for every target but one, no function of the loss that vanishes with it bounds the sampling error.

sections.heading: The frozen chain and existence.
sections.text: The Green operator (Section 3 ): its norm B ^ \widehat{B} is the constant of the paper, bounded through the hitting times of backward trajectories or through mixing. Existence on finite graphs (Section 4 ): on a finite path-connected graph, for each target positive on the stopping states, a backward policy positive on the edges has a balanced flow that samples it exactly ( Morozov et al., 2025 ) , here the invariant measure of the loop closure. L p L^{p} -universality (Section 4 ): on a general state space a frozen backward policy with summable mixing has flows universal in L p L^{p} , exactly so in L ∞ L^{\infty} — the one place where the mixing sum, and not B ^ \widehat{B} , is the price.

sections.heading: Gradient descent diffuses the flow (Section 5 ).
sections.text: Gradient as diffusion : near balance the gradient of the flow-matching loss on a graph applies the backward chain’s I − P I-P twice, once through its adjoint. Curvature and local rate : near balance the curvature of the flow-matching loss is of order 1 / B ^ 2 1/\widehat{B}^{2} from both sides, and training on the flow-matching and detailed-balance losses converges at a rate at least of that order, linearized on any state space and in full on a finite graph. Global convergence : the ( log ⁡ x ) 2 (\log x)^{2} balance loss on states converges from every positive initialization on a finite path-connected graph, at a rate read off backward trajectories and with no mixing hypothesis. Non-monotonicity : freezing buys curvature, not stability; a circulation can still lower these losses, and for strictly unimodal generators gaining circulation is how training reaches balance.

sections.text: The doubling graph : its backward trajectories have finite mean length, the quantity Morozov et al. sections.heading: Evidence.
sections.text: Appendix C confronts most results with exact computation, on state spaces small enough for the sampling error to be a linear solve rather than an estimate, and names those that no measurement reaches yet. Two of these measurements are in the body: the circulation that ratio losses cannot see (Figure 2 ), and the rate of training against its prediction and its guarantee (Figure 3 ).

sections.heading: Certification.
sections.text: Every theorem of the paper is certified in Lean 4 on Mathlib, and no statement’s status is typed by hand: each carries a badge computed from the dependency closure of its Lean declaration. Certified means closed with no axiom beyond propext , Classical.choice and Quot.sound ; a statement resting on scaffolded dependencies would be marked as such, and one whose proof is open typeset as a conjecture. The theorem statements, their badges and every number are generated from the Lean certificate and the experiment results; only the prose is written, and the prose around the statements — remarks, readings, measurements — is not formalized. The body shows the results that carry the story; everything else is unrolled into English in Appendix A , which opens on the proof-structure graph and records how each Lean statement reads the paper’s.

sections.text:
Freezing the backward policy turns training into a question about one Markov chain. A marked graph is a directed graph with a source s 0 s_{0} and a sink s f s_{f} , path-connected when every state lies on a path from s 0 s_{0} to s f s_{f} ; its loop closure adds the wrap edge from s f s_{f} to s 0 s_{0} , and a backward policy π ← \pi_{\leftarrow} extends to a Markov kernel π ^ ← \widehat{\pi}_{\leftarrow} on all its states that steps from s 0 s_{0} to s f s_{f} through the wrap. No aperiodicity is assumed. Where the chain mixes summably, the Green operator is the sum of the centred powers of P P , and B ^ \widehat{B} is at most the mixing sum (Theorem 19 ). For a reversible chain B ^ \widehat{B} is exactly the reciprocal spectral gap ( Levin & Peres, 2017 ) . No loop closure of a marked graph with an internal state is reversible, since the backward chain enters the sink only from the source, through the wrap, while it leaves it towards every terminating state; so for a backward policy the reciprocal gap is a reading and not an identity. The norm B ^ \widehat{B} and the mixing sum differ in general, and the difference matters where the state space is most common: on a leveled graph, where every edge climbs one level — the state space of a fixed-length autoregressive model — the loop closure is periodic, its mixing coefficients do not decay and the mixing sum is infinite (Theorem 51 ), while B ^ \widehat{B} stays finite. This is why the constant of the paper is the norm of the Green operator and not the mixing sum, and why the rates of Section 5 stay informative on fixed-length autoregressive state spaces.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion and limitations
sections.text: The constant that prices training is the norm of the Green operator of the frozen backward chain, and the doubling graph is the reminder that it is not the mean backward length: the mean can be finite where the constant is infinite, and on a truncation the constant grows with the size while the mean does not. The quantity to estimate from the backward trajectories a practitioner already samples is B ^ \widehat{B} — their exit times and visit counts bound it — and not the length of those trajectories; and near balance it bounds the curvature of the loss from both sides. The theory is global only where it is tabular, on finite graphs; in the parameterized case the rates are untested, and only the certificate has been checked along training (Appendix C ). The rates are proved for the ratio losses that are trained, the certificates for difference losses: at the limit of training the sampler is exact, but nothing here shows that a difference loss falls along the way. The backward policy is frozen, not trained: training it, and choosing it for its constant, are future work, with no claim made here. No rate is proved for trajectory balance, only a step cap. One boundary case of the doubling chain’s phase diagram is open. What the paper does settle is which loss to watch, what its value certifies, and what sets the speed at which it falls: a difference loss, the L 1 L^{1} norm of the defect, and the Green operator of the chain that training holds fixed.

sections.text: This chapter. A finite path-connected marked graph — a source s 0 s_{0} , a sink s f s_{f} and the set 𝒮 \mathcal{S} of internal states between them — with a backward policy positive on its edges, closed into a loop by the wrap edge s f → s 0 s_{f}\rightarrow s_{0} . The objects are the invariant probability λ \lambda of the loop-closed backward chain, the flows it generates, and the sampler of the generative flow obtained by cutting the wrap. That a positive frozen backward policy on a finite graph determines a balanced flow, through the expected backward visits, is due to Morozov et al. (2025) , and on acyclic graphs to Bengio et al. What this chapter adds is a proof through the invariant measure of the backward loop closure, in the reading of Deleu & Bengio (2023) , and the certificate. sections.text: Theorem 54 . The loop closure is irreducible, and every invariant probability of it is positive at every state. Proof. The graph half is a pair of explicit paths reach_all_none . Every state reaches the ladder state 1 1 : from a ladder state the decrements walk down to the source, the wrap carries it to the sink, and the target row re-enters the ladder. Conversely 1 1 reaches every state, by climbing: from n n the doubling edge to 2 ​ n 2n followed by n − 1 n-1 decrements lands on n + 1 n+1 , and 2 ​ n ≥ n + 1 2n\geq n+1 . Concatenating the two gives reachability between any pair. The measure half is general PreStat.pos_of_irreducible : an invariant probability is positive somewhere, and invariance transports that positivity along any path, so irreducibility spreads it over the whole state space. ∎ Irreducibility and positivity are the standing hypotheses under which the rest of this chapter speaks of the invariant probability and of the operators built from it. The main text’s universality and convergence theorems are stated for chains carrying such a measure; what follows establishes, for each member of the family, whether one exists. Theorem 55 . Let ε = ε c , s \varepsilon=\varepsilon_{c,s} with c > 0 c>0 , in the standing range. The loop closure has an invariant probability if s > 1 s>1 , or s = 1 s=1 and c < 1 c<1 ; it has none if s < 1 s<1 , or s = 1 s=1 and c ≥ 1 c\geq 1 . Proof. Four cases, each a drift computation against a Lyapunov function, and no more. sections.heading: Appendix C Experimental grounding of the Lean theorems
sections.text: The Lean certificate settles whether each statement of this paper holds; no measurement can add to that. What a measurement can add is of another kind: the size of a constant a theorem leaves unspecified, a prediction the theorem makes and an experiment confirms, the place where a certified bound becomes vacuous or its hypothesis fails, or a view of the mechanism a proof constructs. Table C names the six forms this takes, and fixes how the body may phrase each; a check , which evaluates a certified inequality on instances, is the weakest of them, since a violation would indict the code or the reading of a Lean statement as the paper’s, never the proof. The statements are grouped as in the reading map of the certificate, a finer division of the results than the map of Figure 1 , each with its certification badge and its Lean declarations. Every number below is computed from the experiment results at the pinned commit of the experiment sub-repository, never typed; a measurement that has been run but is not in the pin is listed as pending, without its numbers, and a statement no measurement bears on is listed as such. Discrepancies between a result file and the lab record that are not yet resolved are flagged on the entries they affect and stated at the end.
